title: Mixed-precision edgecases: Qwen MoE token-boundary latency investigation
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a weird latency pattern we saw when running Qwen MoE models with mixed-precision paths (fp16 + 4-bit quantized FFN kernels) on long-context workloads. Observed: intermittent 10–40ms p99 spikes at sequence boundaries (tokenizers boundaries and prompt concatenation points) even when aggregate throughput looked fine. Spikes correlate with routing fanout variance and occasional CUDA pagefault-like stalls.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture experiment matrix and heuristics for reproducing
- Hypotheses for root cause (ordering of kernel selection, allocator churn at token boundary, small-batch kernel fallback)
- Short action list for follow-ups and temporary mitigations

Environment & baseline:
- Model: qwen-14b-moe (2-expert-per-token config used for these runs)
- Runtime: redwood-serving v0.61.2 (local build with mixed-precision kernel switcher)
- HW: A100-sXM-80GB, PCIe interconnect to host, CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.0
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04
- Input workload: long-context chat traces (avg seq len 6k tokens, tail to 12k). Tokenization uses sentencepiece v0.1.96, tokenization boundary means end-of-chunk merges when streaming.
- Batching: auto-batch window 8ms; dynamic routing with per-request canary enabled
- Quantization: FFN/linear layers quantized to 4-bit using asymmetric group quantization (QAT weights, per-channel scales). KV-cache uses fp16.

How it was first noticed:
- Canary test: 500k requests over 24h to a single dedicated node. Overall p50/p90/p99 looked within SLO, but SRE alerted on occasional 10–40ms p99 jitter increases localized to windows where requests had recent prompt attachments (i.e., concatenated prompts with a boundary token). Sampled traces showed stalled GPU kernels around the router and FFN handoff.

Reproduction steps (fast):
1) Start single node with the same runtime flags as production: --enable-mmix --auto-batching-ms=8 --router-concurrency=4 --quant-profile=group4-asym
2) Use the reproduction harness (scripts/profiles/repro_qwen_moe_token_boundary.py) to send ~50k long-context requests, half with appended prompt chunk (explicit boundary marker) and half without
3) Capture per-request traces (x-trace) and nvprof traces for a subset
4) Examine timeline around boundary token positions (where tokenizer returns a glue token or abruptly changes segmentation)

Observed signals:
- Kernel timeline: short (<1ms) kernel launches spike in frequency around the boundary token; the runtime switches from a fused-FFN kernel to a fallback path for some micro-batches causing extra kernel launches and small DMA ops
- Memory churn: small allocator calls (cudaMallocAsync/free) observed around the same time in ~2% of requests, correlated with when group-quantized FFN falls back to non-quant kernel due to alignment mismatch (channel count vs group size mismatch after padding at boundary)
- Router behavior: token-level fanout variance increases (some tokens briefly route to 4 experts instead of 2) when the tokenizer produces split tokens at boundary; this increases intermediate activation traffic and triggers small tensor reshapes that the quantized kernels don't handle efficiently
- Temperature of GPU: no thermal throttling; utilization remains high. No OOMs.

Micro-benchmarks run locally:
- Isolated FFN kernels (quantized vs fp16) across shapes: when seq_len % 8 != 0 (common at boundary slices) the quantized kernel shows 8–20% slowdown and higher jitter due to scalar tail-path handling
- Router serialize step: small-batch (batches of <4 tokens) increases overhead of expert handshake by ~0.6ms/request vs expected ~0.2ms

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Kernel selection mismatch at boundary shapes: our kernel selector picks a group-quantized kernel assuming packed layout; boundary tokenization yields different effective shapes requiring a fallback that is more expensive and causes extra allocations.
2) Small-batch routing amplification: tokenization boundaries create micro-batches with skewed token distributions; router handshake + expert scatter becomes sensitive to quantization code-paths and increases kernel count.
3) Allocator fragmentation / host<->device DMA: occasional cudaMallocAsync/free pattern suggests an unhandled path where temporary buffers are allocated when kernel fallback occurs, adding 1–5ms latency for some requests.
4) Sparse-hotspot and cache invalidation: tokens at boundary skew attention patterns, evicting small local caches used by fused kernels and causing re-materialization costs.

Evidence supporting hypothesis 1 & 2:
- Replaying the exact token sequences but forcing a consistent padding to shapes aligned to 8 eliminated the 10–40ms spikes in the sampled trace window
- Forcing router to fixed-expert-per-token (disable dynamic fanout) reduced p99 spikes by ~60%
- Instrumenting kernel-selector showed 95% of spiky requests hit quantized->fallback transitions within a 2-step window of the boundary token

Quick experiments tried and outcomes:
- Force-aligned padding (pad to 8): reduces spikes but increases average token compute cost by ~4% and overall throughput drop; acceptable as a debug lever but not great in prod
- Disable quantized FFN fallback (force fp16 for all FFNs): eliminates spikes but increases token cost by ~22% (regression in cost)
- Increase auto-batch window to 16ms: reduces spikes (more stable shapes) but worsens median latency for short queries; tradeoff unacceptable for p50-oriented customers
- Add small persistent scratch buffer pool to avoid cudaMallocAsync: cut per-event malloc stalls but didn't remove root cause; still see kernel fallback overhead

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why does tokenizer boundary cause the group-quantized kernel to consider layout incompatible? Is it pad-size only or something deeper in shape inference? Need to trace shape metadata in kernel-selector path.
- Are there heuristics in our routing that prefer additional experts on boundary tokens because of content features? (i.e., content-based gating could be correlated)
- Is there any interaction with nvFuser kernel generation where tiny kernels cause suboptimal codegen?

Next steps (short):
- Add logging in kernel-selector to capture pre/post shape hashes for any quantized->fallback transitions (PR: runtime/#789) — Claire to own 
- Run targeted fuzz: mutate sequences by inserting boundary-like tokens to find minimal reproduction case (Samir)
- Expand persistent scratch pool to cover fallback path allocations and measure effect (Miguel)
- Add routing instrumentation to show per-token gate logits for sequences that trigger spiky fanout (Aditi)

Longer-term mitigations to consider:
- Make quantized kernels tolerant to tail-pad shapes (implement generic tail-handling inside kernel instead of host fallback) — high payoff but moderately invasive
- Router smoothing: add tiny gate temperature / rolling-average to avoid transient fanout changes due to token boundary artifacts
- Shape choir: pre-pad sequences to canonical shapes for batches only when latency SLO allows, or use per-request adaptive padding policies
- Compiler-level: investigate nvFuser fallback for tiny kernels and whether tensorization thresholds are tuned properly for 4-bit kernels

Notes / stray observations:
- This pattern shows up more commonly when we have streaming concatenation between user prompt + LLM system prompt; full prompt merge (single tokenization pass) reduces occurrences dramatically — suggests partial-tokenization and on-the-fly concatenation is a major factor
- Small but repeated observation: when mixed-precision path triggers fallback, p99 spikes often coincide with small host-side CPU spikes (1–3ms) in scheduler thread; likely coordination cost of launching extra kernels and updating profiling counters

Immediate recommendations for prod shielding:
1) Add a lightweight feature flag to force per-request padding to 8 when request has streaming-concatenate flag set (low risk, opt-in)
2) Backstop: detect quantized->fallback transitions in telemetry and route affected traffic to fp16 path for the next N requests from that customer to avoid repeated spikes

Appendix: useful trace excerpts (reformatted)
- Example trace id: trace-20250208-1345-39
  timeline (abridged): host-sched 0.3ms -> kernel-launch fused-ffn-quant 0.8ms -> cudaMallocAsync 1.9ms -> kernel-launch ffn-fallback 2.6ms -> nvtx:router-handshake 0.6ms -> done

- Example trace id: trace-20250212-0932-11 (no spike): host-sched 0.2ms -> kernel-launch fused-ffn-quant 0.7ms -> kernel-launch kv-update 0.4ms -> done
